newsitem.title: USA: Hydro Magnesium to step up imports to US.
newsitem.headline: Hydro Magnesium to step up imports to US.

text.p: Hydro Magnesium, a division of Norway's Norsk Hydro, said it is renewing ties with past pure magnesium customers in the U.S. as it plans to step up imports of the metal from its Canadian plant.

Last month U.S. Commerce Dept provisionally cut to zero from 21 percent the dumping duty on imports of Hydro's pure magnesium from its Quebec-based Becancour plant into the U.S. following a review of the small lots imported at present.

"We would like to get back to our traditional customers, so we are reviewing that internally and with our customers to decide how to do that," said Robert Edgar, Hydro Magnesium's vice-president of marketing.
"We were importing small amounts and we will gradually raise that,' Edgar added.

Hydro's higher imports are unlikely to disrupt the market -- the company will be anxious to charge higher prices than traders to avoid any dumping accusations -- but some traders are likely to lose tonnages, dealers said.
"It's a threat to us to some extent, yes," a magnesium importer said.
Two further review periods of Hydro's imports will be undertaken by Commerce before any final dumping duty ruling is made.

But how much pure magnesium Hydro will have to export to the U.S. remains to be seen. The company is expanding production of alloy magnesium at Becancour, which it sells in large quantities to the U.S. already. There is no dumping duty on Canadian alloy.
And Edgar said earlier this year the market for pure magnesium was mature, with alloy for diecast auto parts offering the best growth prospects.
Pure magnesium is used to make the more expensive alloy magnesium even though pure prices are higher.
Hydro cut its European pure magnesium list price earlier this week, but Edgar said the company would not be lowering its U.S. price of $1.94 per pound.
"Prices are stable in the U.S. for us, and alloy is stable in both markets, Europe and the U.S.," Edgar said.
Traders said spot, imported magnesium prices were in the $1.56 to $1.64 per pound range. U.S. producers were said to be selling any surplus pure spot material for about $1.70 per lb.

"Things look a little bit better in the U.S. and we have made some decent sales this past week," a trader said. "We are starting to get inquiries for the fourth quarter and next year from Canada as well."
The trader suggested that major consumers were looking to buy more long-term contract metal from traders than from producers in 1997. The "showdown" for this business begins later this month.
Traders and Hydro noted some improved business in Europe, and felt destocking among consumers was over with talk of production difficulties at one unnamed producer.
Edgar said that in Europe "we are starting to see some pick up in the steel industry with desulfurization. This indicates to us we may see a strengthening in the fourth quarter."
Recent International Magnesium Association figures showed that global inventory rose to 33,400 tonnes by the end of June. "This is still less than a month's supply," Edgar said.
